A virtual function is a member function where the call goes to the version the object's actual type overrides, not the type of the pointer or reference used to call it. The type the compiler sees at the call site is the static type; the type of the object really there is the dynamic type, and a virtual call through a base pointer or reference reaches the dynamic type's version. The compiler arranges this with a vtable, one per class with virtual functions, holding that class's override addresses, and a vptr, a hidden pointer in every such object pointing at its class's table.

The problem this solves is writing code once against a base class that keeps working for every class that implements it, including ones written after that code was compiled, as long as each keeps the base's promises. Without virtual dispatch, a function taking a base reference always calls the base's own version, whatever the caller passed.

The mechanism is that a constructor sets the vptr as each base finishes building and each derived class takes over, so a virtual call made from a base's own constructor still reaches the base's version, never a derived one not yet built. A call through the base becomes an indirect call: load the vptr, load the function's address out of the table, and call through it.

What it costs is more than the call itself. A base held by pointer needs a virtual destructor, or deleting through the base skips every derived destructor, and a base that stays copyable slices: copying through the base type keeps only the base part, silently, because the copy is a complete object of the base's own type. Composition sidesteps dispatch by holding behaviour instead of inheriting it, as a closed
of the possible kinds or an open
of the possible behaviours: a class hierarchy is cheap to extend with a new kind and expensive to give a new operation, and a variant is the other way round.
You meet this in a robot's sensor list, a
of owned interfaces a control loop reports through without knowing which is a lidar and which is a sonar, and it's the interview question itself: why a base pointed to by a
needs a virtual destructor, and what happens when a derived object is passed by value into a function expecting the base.
